consultation:
Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s vision or eyes.
Parent: I'm worried about his eyes, he often squints when looking at things and it seems like he's having trouble focusing. I've noticed it more when he's trying to watch TV or play with toys that have small parts.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child's hearing or ears.
Parent: Yes, he's had a glue ear before, and we've had to take him to the doctor a few times to get it drained. It seems to happen when he gets a cold or after swimming.

Doctor: Please tell us about the problems with your child’s teeth.
Parent: His front teeth are quite large compared to other kids his age. We've been told to keep an eye on them to make sure they don't cause any problems with his bite or speech.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s heart.
Parent: The doctor said he needs regular heart check-ups because of a concern they found. I'm not entirely sure what it is, but we go back every few months for another look.

Doctor: Please tell us about any neurological problem your child has (brain, nerves, muscle tone, fits).
Parent: He was slower to start walking and sitting up compared to his siblings. Even now at 3 years old he still struggles with balance sometimes.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child's kidneys.
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s immune system (ability to fight infection and vaccination responses).
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child’s gastrointestinal system (feeding, stomach, bowel).
Parent: He has constipation issues occasionally. Sometimes he'll go days without going to the bathroom and then have a hard time passing stool. We try to give him more fiber and fluids.

Doctor: Please use this box to tell us about any other medical problems that you haven’t been able to mention above.
Parent: He has shorter fingers than average and his spine curves slightly to one side which the doctors call scoliosis. They said it might need monitoring as he grows older.
report:
# CLINICAL PATIENT REPORT

## 1) RESPIRATORY

a) How this affects the patient:
- N/A

b) How this affects others with the syndrome:
- Children with KBG syndrome may experience respiratory issues, including recurrent otitis media (middle ear infections) and temporary blockage of the Eustachian tubes (glue ear). These can lead to temporary hearing loss and frequent visits to the ENT (Ear, Nose, and Throat) clinic.
- Management Recommendations:
  - Regular ENT check-ups to monitor for potential issues.
  - Addressing glue ear promptly with ventilation tubes (grommets) as needed.

## 2) CARDIOLOGY

a) How this affects the patient:
- N/A

b) How this affects others with the syndrome:
- Children with KBG syndrome are at risk of congenital heart defects, particularly valve abnormalities and atrial septal defect (ASD). These can result in various heart-related issues, including persistent patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), ventricular septal defect (VSD), and other structural anomalies.
- Management Recommendations:
  - Regular cardiac evaluations, including echocardiography and EKG, to monitor for and address any heart-related issues.
  - Follow-up care with a pediatric cardiologist as recommended.

## 3) GASTROENTEROLOGY

a) How this affects the patient:
- N/A

b) How this affects others with the syndrome:
- Children with KBG syndrome commonly experience feeding difficulties, including refusal to eat solids, vomiting, and regurgitation. These issues can contribute to nutritional deficiencies and delayed milestones.
- Management Recommendations:
  - Consulting with a pediatric gastroenterologist for dietary assessment and possible interventions such as enteral nutrition via a feeding tube.
  - Ensuring adequate hydration and electrolyte balance, especially in infants and young children.

## 4) IMMUNOLOGY

a) How this affects the patient:
- N/A

b) How this affects others with the syndrome:
- Individuals with KBG syndrome are at increased risk of developing autoimmune diseases, including Type 1 diabetes mellitus, thyroid disease, and inflammatory bowel disease. They may also be more susceptible to allergic reactions and immunological challenges.
- Management Recommendations:
  - Regular screening for autoimmune markers and early intervention if autoimmune issues are identified.
  - Monitoring for and managing allergies and sensitivities.

## 5) NEUROLOGY

a) How this affects the patient:
- N/A

b) How this affects others with the syndrome:
- Children with KBG syndrome frequently exhibit developmental delays, behavioral differences, and learning difficulties. They may display autistic-like behaviors, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and sensory integration dysfunction.
- Management Recommendations:
  - Implementing strategies to support cognitive, sensory, and motor development.
  - Considering educational and therapeutic interventions tailored to the child’s unique needs.

## 6) EAR NOSE THROAT

a) How this affects the patient:
- N/A

b) How this affects others with the syndrome:
- Children with KBG syndrome are prone to recurrent otitis media (ear infections) and glue ear (build-up of fluid in the ear), leading to temporary hearing loss and frequent audiologic assessments.
- Management Recommendations:
  - Prompt treatment of glue ear with ventilation tubes (grommets) as needed.
  - Encouraging good hygiene practices to reduce the likelihood of future infections.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION

a) How this affects the patient:
- N/A

b) How this affects others with the syndrome:
- Children with KBG syndrome are at increased risk of vision problems, including short-sightedness (hypermetropia), astigmatism, and refractive errors. Glue ear (otosome) can exacerbate these issues.
- Management Recommendations:
  - Regular ophthalmic examinations to monitor vision and address any underlying conditions.
  - Addressing glue ear promptly with ventilation tubes (grommets) as needed.

## 8) DERMATOLOGY

a) How this affects the patient:
- N/A

b) How this affects others with the syndrome:
- Children with KBG syndrome may develop skin conditions such as eczema, keratosis pilaris, and acneiform eruptions. Their immune systems may react differently to vaccines and medications.
- Management Recommendations:
  - Keeping the skin moisturized and applying emollients as directed.
  - Following vaccine schedules and considering allergy testing prior to vaccinations.

## 9) DENTAL

a) How this affects the patient:
- N/A

b) How this affects others with the syndrome:
- Children with KBG syndrome are at increased risk of tooth decay (dental caries) due to their larger molars and habit of sucking their thumbs. They may also experience bruxism (teeth grinding) and hypodontia (missing teeth).
- Management Recommendations:
  - Implementing a thorough oral hygiene routine, including fluoride applications and sealants.
  - Advising against thumb sucking beyond the age of two, as it can increase the risk of cavities.

## 10) EDUCATION

a) How this affects the patient:
- N/A

b) How this affects others with the syndrome:
- Educationally, children with KBG syndrome may require additional support in the classroom, including modifications to curriculum requirements and provision of assistive devices such as orthotic splints and communication aids.
- Management Recommendations:
  - Providing a suitable educational setting, whether mainstream or specialist.
  - Utilizing Individual Education Plans (IEPs) and accommodations as per the child’s needs.

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT

a) How this affects the patient:
- N/A

b) How this affects others with the syndrome:
- Behaviourally, children with KBG syndrome may exhibit characteristics of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), including repetitive behavior, difficulty with transitions, and social interaction challenges. Learning-wise, they may struggle with fine motor skills, coordination, and sensory processing.
- Management Recommendations:
  - Implementing strategies to enhance sensory integration and proprioception.
  - Engaging in sensory therapies and occupational therapy sessions.

## 12) SKELETAL

a) How this affects the patient:
- N/A

b) How this affects others with the syndrome:
- Skeletally, children with KBG syndrome are at increased risk of skeletal anomalies, including brachydactyly (short fingers) and clinodactyly (curved fifth finger). They may also experience irregular bone development, specifically in the spine (scoliosis) and hips (hip dysplasia).
- Management Recommendations:
  - Regular X-rays and physical examination to monitor bone density and assess the progression of scoliosis.
  - Consider orthopedic evaluation and consideration of corrective surgeries as needed.

## 13) RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SCREENING AND TREATMENTS
- Regular ENT check-ups to monitor for glue ear and address potential issues.
- Consultation with a pediatric cardiologist for ongoing cardiovascular evaluations.
- Dietary assessment and possible enteral nutrition via a feeding tube.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s vision or eyes.
Parent: Oh, yes... our child has hypermetropia, which means his eyes are turned inward slightly. It's been a concern since birth, really. I worry about how it might affect his everyday life, like playing catch or watching TV. We've had multiple appointments with specialists already.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child's hearing or ears.
Parent: There's fluid in his ear, which has caused some discomfort and pain. We've taken him to see an ENT specialist a few times now. They've tried a couple of treatments to clear it out. Poor baby gets so upset when it flares up. 

Doctor: Please tell us about the problems with your child’s teeth.
Parent: His teeth... well, they're very weak, especially the enamel. I make sure he brushes them gently and uses a child-friendly toothpaste. But still, there are cavities. It's hard to see him in pain, even if it's just a small filling. 

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s heart.
Parent: Yes, unfortunately. There's an abnormality with one of the valves. We go back to the cardiologist regularly for check-ups. They monitor it closely to ensure everything stays stable. As a parent, it's terrifying to think about, but we're managing so far. 

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child's hormones.
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about any neurological problem your child has (brain, nerves, muscle tone, fits).
Parent: He was born with a tethered cord. That's meant lots of monitoring over time to ensure no lasting damage occurred. So far, touch wood, he seems okay, though we do have regular scans to confirm. 

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child's kidneys.
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s immune system (ability to fight infection and vaccination responses).
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child’s gastrointestinal system (feeding, stomach, bowel).
Parent: He experiences bowel problems sometimes. This causes him, and us, a lot of distress. Changing diets and keeping an eye on what he eats helps manage it a bit better. But yes, it's definitely something we need to stay on top of. 

Doctor: Please use this box to tell us about any other medical problems that you haven’t been able to mention above.
Parent: Undescended testes were another thing. Something we discovered after birth and have kept track of ever since. Specialists keep saying it might correct itself over time, but until then, we'll continue these regular hospital visits.

# CLINICAL PATIENT REPORT

## 1) RESPIRATORY

a) How this affects the patient:
- None noted.

b) How this affects others with the syndrome:
- Children with KBG syndrome commonly experience respiratory issues, including recurrent otitis media (middle ear infections) and nasal congestion. These can lead to breathing difficulties and require frequent medical attention.
- Regular ENT (ear, nose, throat) evaluations and possible antibiotic treatments are recommended to address these issues.
- Monitoring for potential complications such as glue ear (fluid buildup in the ear) and sinus infections is crucial.

## 2) CARDIOLOGY

a) How this affects the patient:
- The presence of a tethered cord requires ongoing monitoring and potential interventions, such as MRI examinations and physical therapy.
- Regular follow-up with a pediatric cardiologist is essential to manage any congenital heart defects or valve abnormalities.
- Management strategies include medication, observation, and, in some cases, surgical intervention.

b) How this affects others with the syndrome:
- Children with KBG syndrome are at risk of developing heart conditions, including valve abnormalities and structural heart defects.
- Regular echocardiograms and EKGs are recommended to monitor heart health and detect potential issues early.
- Follow-up care includes consultations with pediatric cardiologists and consideration of surgical options for valve repair or replacement.

## 3) GASTROENTEROLOGY

a) How this affects the patient:
- The presence of macrodontia (large permanent upper middle teeth) can lead to orthodontic issues requiring treatment.
- Frequent dental cleanings and close monitoring of tooth decay and gum disease are necessary.
- Orthodontic evaluation and potential corrective procedures may be considered based on the severity of the condition.

b) How this affects others with the syndrome:
- Individuals with KBG syndrome often exhibit macrodontia, leading to orthodontic challenges such as difficulty cleaning between teeth and potential dental abscesses.
- Regular dental hygiene practices and monitoring for periodontal issues are critical components of management.

## 4) IMMUNOLOGY

a) How this affects the patient:

b) How this affects others with the syndrome:
- Immunological concerns, particularly regarding the immune response to vaccines, are a significant factor in the management of KBG syndrome.
